extracted.intended_audience: journalism students, media scholars, and newsroom editors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and analytic criteria used by magazines and network newsrooms to decide which stories to publish or air, how to edit sources, and how to measure audience response. Covers newsworthiness, editorial norms (editing quotations/language), pacing and lead construction, sourcing for trends, competition/scooping, and use of audience metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing public figures' language
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors routinely correct or modify the syntax, dialectal markers, or ethnic language in quotations from public figures to avoid making them 'look bad' unless the language itself is newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: an editor 'had to correct her bad syntax and take out her Yiddishisms; otherwise, people will think we are trying to make her look bad.' Apply corrections to preserve perceived fairness to the speaker unless the phrasing is central to the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction of profanity and slurs except when newsworthy
rubrics_metrics.description: Public officials who use profanity or racial/ethnic slurs are automatically 'corrected' in publication, except when their resort to such language itself becomes newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When slurs/profanity reveal misconduct or become a moral-disorder story (e.g., Earl Butz, Nixon tapes), retain them and treat the language as the news hook; otherwise sanitize to avoid gratuitous offense and to prevent perceived unfairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical-component test for story suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists may assume a present abnormality is newsworthy by construing it against a stipulated ideal past normality; expectations often include an implicit historical component.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters and editors may frame events as 'new' by inventing or presuming a prior normal state; be aware this rhetorical move can manufacture newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign governmental change: violence threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: For most foreign countries (except the most important allied or Communist states), governmental change is considered newsworthy only when it involves violent protest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonviolent governmental change in distant or less-prominent countries is often excluded unless violence occurs; prioritize coverage when protests turn violent or have clear regional/global implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-interest stories selected for audience aid/engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Magazines and networks sometimes choose human-interest stories with the explicit or implicit goal of prompting audience financial help or emotional engagement; objectivity may be relaxed to solicit aid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors accept violations of detachment when audience contributions or clear audience engagement are likely, seeing the response as evidence the audience is paying attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pace and 'feel' as news-judgment criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: News judgment relies partly on an intuitive 'feel' — including editors' and writers' evaluations of pacing and avoidance of boredom — when selecting and shaping stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recruit and use staff able to sense audience attention; pacing decisions (e.g., where to place big points) are made informally but shape story selection and treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and catching the crest of a story
rubrics_metrics.description: Magazines typically attempt to catch stories 'as they crest' — picking up trends at their peak — but may err by writing about them after the peak has passed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for timeliness: select and publish while a story or trend is cresting. Beware of late trend pieces that report the 'dwindling foam after the wave went home.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Sourcing sufficiency for trend claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Trend or social-change pieces require adequate, geographically and socially representative sourcing; small, unrepresentative samples can create misleading 'trend' stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a bisexuality trend was asserted on nine mostly coastal/professional sources; avoid broad claims based on limited or skewed sources and note sampling limits in the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead construction and placement of 'big gongs' at top
rubrics_metrics.description: Story structure should 'put the big gongs [points] at the top' — begin with the major points and use leads that set the tone (sentimental or high-energy); magazines may assign tonal metaphors to leads (e.g., Newsweek's 'violin').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use strong, clear opening that highlights the central conflict or emotional pull; recognize different tonal strategies ('high tones' for sentiment) and ensure the lead matches audience expectations and section norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between film and tell stories (TV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Television newsrooms maintain an informal balance between film-heavy stories and 'tell' (anchor/narration) stories to preserve the anchor's role and program variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers monitor mix of filmed pieces and studio narration; avoid overloading with one format which could reduce the anchor to a mere host or bore viewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition to scoop (speed and exclusivity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Top producers and editors try to 'scoop' rivals by being first to film a breaking story or by sending prominent personnel (e.g., anchorpersons) to personal-report on events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize speed and exclusivity in newsgathering operations when resources allow; coordinate fast deployment and clearances to secure first reports or exclusive interviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of internal memos for sensational but unconfirmed items
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsmagazines issue internal memos filled with sensational stories that cannot be published because supporting evidence is unavailable; these memos sometimes serve as entertainment for top editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat memo items as leads-to-investigate rather than publishable copy; be cautious about elevating memo items into run stories without corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring cover choices via newsstand sales
rubrics_metrics.description: Top editors use newsstand sale-figures (their own and rivals') to monitor audience reaction to cover choices and adjust packaging and editorial emphasis accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult sales and circulation data when deciding covers and major package treatments; cover selection balances editorial judgment and commercial data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on audience-research firms (Nielsen, Simmons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsrooms and magazines rely on external audience-research (Nielsen for TV ratings; Simmons for magazine reader demographics) to understand viewer/reader characteristics and to target content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Nielsen for frequency/audience size and Simmons for detailed reader/viewer characteristics; interpret the data (and its limitations) when planning content and marketing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anchorperson as primary audience attractor
rubrics_metrics.description: A substantial share of viewers choose network news based on the anchorperson (studies cite about 40% in some samples), making anchor popularity a key programming factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in anchor selection and retention as a strategic means to retain/attract audiences; recognize anchor-driven loyalty and its influence on scheduling and presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for audience distraction and partial attention
rubrics_metrics.description: A significant portion of TV news audiences watch with distractions (reading, talking, eating), so producers must account for variable attention when constructing programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design segments and pacing for intermittent attention: use clear hooks, repeat key points, and place salient information early to reach viewers who may not watch the whole program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial selection and treatment of reader letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters departments filter incoming mail, using form letters for most responses, while editors select the most interesting and articulate letters to publish as a way of reflecting tone and volume of audience reaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a story provokes significant mail, lead with emphatic or representative letters to convey both tone and quantity of response; track letter volume and content as an audience-feedback metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial input on packaging vs editorial control of content
rubrics_metrics.description: Business-department research and recommendations (e.g., cover redesign) may influence packaging and presentation, but editors typically retain final decisions about which stories run.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use commercial research to inform packaging while maintaining editorial autonomy over content selection and news judgment; document boundaries between business input and editorial authority.
